title: AI Foundations: 6 Live Classes
blurb: The practical introduction for busy professionals. Six 90-minute classes take you from first prompt to a personal AI playbook: how assistants work, the CLEAR prompting framework, checking accuracy, protecting private data, everyday workflows, and a 30-day plan.

modules.t: Class 1 — What AI is, what it isn't, and where it fits in your work
modules.d: A plain-English tour of how AI assistants work, what they do well and badly, how to choose one, and the three rules for using them safely at work.
modules.body:
Why this class comes first

This class gives you a working mental model of AI: what these tools are, where they help in an ordinary workweek, and where they can embarrass you. By the end you will have held a real conversation with an assistant about a task from your own job.

Class agenda (90 minutes)

  • 0:00-0:10 Welcome, introductions, and one task you would love help with
  • 0:10-0:30 How a language model works: prediction, training data, tokens, context
  • 0:30-0:45 Strengths, weak spots, and a live demo of a confident wrong answer
  • 0:45-1:00 The four main assistants, free vs paid, and picking one for this course
  • 1:00-1:10 The 3 Commandments of AI
  • 1:10-1:25 Labs: your first hands-on conversation
  • 1:25-1:30 Debrief and homework

How a large language model works, in plain English

A large language model (LLM) is software that has learned to predict what text comes next. Give it "Please find attached the" and it calculates that "invoice" or "report" is far more likely than "giraffe." Repeat that prediction a few hundred times and you have a paragraph. ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini and Copilot are prediction engines of this kind, wrapped in a chat window. Four ideas explain most of what you will see:

  • Prediction. The model produces the most plausible continuation of your request. Plausible and true usually overlap. When they don't, you get a fluent, confident sentence that is false, called a hallucination.
  • Training data. The model learned its patterns from a very large collection of text: books, websites, code and more. It keeps patterns, and it does not look facts up in a database. Training also stops at a cutoff date, so unless the assistant searches the web it may know nothing about recent events.
  • Tokens. Models read and write in tokens, which are chunks of text a little shorter than an average word. Usage limits and document size limits are counted in tokens.
  • Context. The context window is everything the model can see at one moment: your instructions, any files you attach, and the conversation so far. In a very long chat, early details can drop out of view. A new chat usually starts blank unless a memory feature is turned on.
Key takeaway: think of an assistant as a very well-read drafting partner whose accuracy you have to check. Treat its output like a first draft from a capable new hire: fast, useful, and in need of your review.

What AI does well, and where it lets you down

Usually strong:

  • Drafting and rewriting emails, letters, job postings and reports
  • Summarizing long documents that you supply
  • Explaining an unfamiliar topic at the level you ask for
  • Reformatting: messy notes into a table, a long memo into bullet points

Check closely:

  • Exact facts, statistics, quotations and citations given from memory
  • Anything recent, when the tool has not searched the web
  • Arithmetic across long lists, unless the tool runs a real calculation
  • Your organization's own policies, which it cannot know unless you provide them
  • Decisions that affect someone's job, health, money or grades

The four main assistants, and how to choose

  • ChatGPT (OpenAI): the most widely recognized, a broad general-purpose choice.
  • Claude (Anthropic): often picked for long documents and careful writing.
  • Gemini (Google): connects with Gmail, Docs and the rest of Google Workspace.
  • Microsoft Copilot: built into Word, Excel, Outlook and Teams for organizations that license it.

Features leapfrog each other every few months, so rankings age badly. Choose with three questions:

  1. What has your employer approved? If there is a policy, it wins.
  2. Where does your work already live: Google, Microsoft, or neither?
  3. Which one do you find easiest to read and steer?

Free vs paid. All four have had a free tier that is enough for this course. Paid individual plans have generally cost around US$20 a month (confirm current US and Canadian pricing on each company's site) and typically buy higher usage limits, stronger models and larger file uploads. Business plans usually add admin controls and firmer data commitments. Start free, and upgrade when a limit starts costing you time. On any tier, open the data settings: some consumer plans may use your chats to improve future models unless you opt out.

The 3 Commandments of AI

  1. Investigate, understand, apply. Try the tool yourself, learn how it behaves, then put it to work on real tasks.
  2. Review for hallucinations and keep a human in the loop. You are accountable for everything you send, sign or submit.
  3. Do no harm. Protect private information, and keep a qualified person in charge of decisions that could hurt someone. Depending on your work, laws such as HIPAA (US health information), FERPA (US student records) or PIPEDA (Canadian private-sector privacy) may apply. When unsure, ask your privacy or compliance lead before you paste.

Worked example: a first real conversation

Dana is the office manager at a 12-person accounting firm in Columbus, Ohio. She needs to announce a new time-off process.

First try: "Write an email about our new time-off process." The result is polished and generic, and it invents a 30-day notice rule the firm does not have.

Second try: "I'm the office manager at a 12-person accounting firm. Starting March 1, time-off requests go through a shared calendar form, with two weeks' notice outside tax season. Draft a friendly 120-word email to staff. Add no rules beyond the ones I listed."

Review: Dana checks the date against the partners' memo, deletes a line promising same-day approval, and sends it under her own name. She has practiced all three commandments: she tried the tool, reviewed the draft, and kept staff and client details out of the chat.

Your turn

Open your assistant and run both labs with low-stakes material.

🧪 Interactive Lab — try it now

I'm new to AI assistants. In plain English and under 150 words, explain what you are and how you produce your answers. Then list three kinds of tasks you are good at and three where I should double-check your work. Finish by asking me one question about my job so you can suggest a good first task.

🧪 Interactive Lab — try it now

Here is a routine task from my job: [describe a low-stakes task, with no names or confidential details]. Write a first draft for me. Then, under the heading 'Check before using', list every fact, number or assumption in your draft that I should verify myself.

Homework: use your assistant for three small work tasks before Class 2. Note what helped and what you had to correct.

📚 Glossary

  • Large language model (LLM): software trained on large amounts of text to predict and generate language.
  • Training data: the text a model learned from, which ends at a cutoff date.
  • Token: a chunk of text, often part of a word, that models use to read, write and measure limits.
  • Context window: the amount of text a model can consider at one time.
  • Hallucination: a fluent, confident output that is false or made up.
  • Prompt: the instruction or question you give an AI assistant.
  • Human in the loop: a person reviews and approves AI output before it is used.

📖 References

  • Vaswani, A., et al. (2017). "Attention Is All You Need." Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 30.
  • National Institute of Standards and Technology (2023). Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework (AI RMF 1.0).
  • OpenAI Help Center. "What are tokens and how to count them?"
  • Mata v. Avianca, Inc. (S.D.N.Y. 2023), sanctions order concerning fabricated case citations.
  • Mollick, E. (2024). Co-Intelligence: Living and Working with AI. Portfolio.
  • Current product and pricing pages from OpenAI, Anthropic, Google and Microsoft (features and prices change often).

quiz.q: Priya, a paralegal in Toronto, asks a chatbot for a case supporting her argument. It replies with a confident, well-formatted citation. Why should she still look it up?
opts: Chatbots are blocked from reading any legal material at all
It predicts plausible text, so a citation can look right and not exist
Legal databases charge the chatbot a fee for each case it shows
Canadian cases are stored in a file format that chatbots cannot open or read
quiz.x: Models generate likely-sounding text and do not look cases up, so a tidy citation can be invented. The idea that chatbots are blocked from legal text is false and misses the real risk.

quiz.q: Marcus, an HR coordinator in Denver, has a two-hour chat going about a 60-page handbook. The assistant starts contradicting details it handled correctly at the start. What is the likeliest cause?
opts: The free plan lowers answer quality after the first hour of use
The assistant's training data was updated during the session
The handbook file was deleted from the company's shared drive
The early material has slipped out of the model's context window
quiz.x: A model can see a limited amount of text at once, and in long chats early content can drop out of view. Training data does not change mid-conversation, so that explanation fails.

quiz.q: A school office administrator in Ohio wants a free chatbot to draft parent letters and plans to paste in a spreadsheet of student names and grades. What should she do first?
opts: Split the spreadsheet into smaller pieces so that no single paste is very large
Paste the file but ask the chatbot to keep the contents private
Strip out identifying details and check which tools the district allows
Use a personal account so the district is not linked to the chat
quiz.x: Student records may fall under FERPA and district policy, so removing identifiers and using an approved tool comes first. Asking a chatbot to keep things private changes nothing about how the data is handled.

quiz.q: Elise runs a four-person bakery in Halifax and is unsure whether to pay for an AI subscription. She has used an assistant twice. Which plan fits this course's advice?
opts: Use a free tier on real tasks, then upgrade if limits slow her down
Buy an annual plan now, since yearly billing is usually cheaper
Subscribe to all four assistants for a month and compare them
Wait a year for prices to drop before trying any of the tools
quiz.x: Free tiers cover beginner needs, and real use shows whether limits matter to her. Paying for four subscriptions at once costs money before she knows what she needs.

quiz.q: In January, an accountant in Winnipeg asks an assistant for this year's federal tax bracket thresholds. It answers instantly from memory with no web search. What is the main risk?
opts: The figures may be from before its training cutoff and now be outdated
The assistant may have rounded each threshold up or down to the nearest dollar
The assistant may have converted the amounts into US dollars
The figures may be correct but arranged in an unfamiliar table
quiz.x: Training stops at a cutoff date, so remembered figures that change yearly can be stale. Rounding or layout issues are minor next to using last year's thresholds.

quiz.q: A grant writer at a Seattle nonprofit asks an assistant for a statistic on local housing need. It supplies a precise percentage and names a county report. What does Commandment 2 require?
opts: Round the percentage so that a small error will not matter
Add a footnote saying the statistic was produced by an AI tool
Ask the same assistant whether it is fully confident in that number
Find the figure in the original report before it goes in the grant
quiz.x: Reviewing for hallucinations means confirming the number in the source itself. Asking the assistant if it is confident is weaker, because it can be confidently wrong twice.

quiz.q: Jasmine, a marketing assistant in Vancouver, has four tasks this week and wants to hand one to an AI assistant. Which one best matches what these tools do well?
opts: Totaling sales tax on 300 orders with no one checking the math
Turning her bullet points into a first draft of the newsletter
Deciding which of two contractors should have a contract ended
Confirming today's exchange rate for a US supplier's latest invoice
quiz.x: Drafting from material she supplies is a core strength and easy for her to review. Live exchange rates need a current source, which a model's memory cannot provide.

quiz.q: A customer service manager in Atlanta has read about AI but has not used it. He wants his team of 15 answering customers with a chatbot starting tomorrow. What does Commandment 1 suggest?
opts: Have the vendor's sales rep confirm the chatbot is accurate
Launch tomorrow and collect complaints to find the weak points
Try it himself on low-stakes tasks, then run a small pilot
Ask the team to vote on whether they trust the new chatbot
quiz.x: Investigate, understand, apply means learning how the tool behaves before relying on it. Launching and waiting for complaints puts customers in the position of testers.

quiz.q: A recruiter at a Dallas logistics firm proposes having an assistant read 400 resumes and send rejection emails automatically, with no person reviewing its choices. What is the best response?
opts: Approve it, since the assistant reads resumes faster than staff
Approve it if rejected applicants are told an AI was involved
Let AI reject applicants but have staff write the emails by hand
Let AI summarize resumes while a person makes each decision
quiz.x: Do no harm keeps a person responsible for decisions that affect livelihoods, with AI in a support role. Disclosure alone does not fix unreviewed or biased rejections.

quiz.q: A clinic in Calgary runs on Microsoft 365, and its IT lead has approved Copilot for staff. A receptionist asks which assistant she should use for work documents. What is the soundest advice?
opts: The newest assistant on the market, since newer models know more
A personal account on any tool, to keep work and IT separate
The approved tool, since it fits her files and the clinic's policy
Whichever assistant ranked highest in last month's technology reviews
quiz.x: Employer approval and fit with where her work lives outweigh rankings, which change every few months. A personal account sidesteps the clinic's safeguards for sensitive information.

facts.t: OpenAI's rule of thumb for the length of one token in English.

labs.title: Where does AI fit in this workweek?
labs.intro: An office manager at a property management firm in Portland listed her week. Place each task in the right bucket.
buckets: Check policy or keep a person in charge
items: Rewrite a blunt email to a vendor so it sounds courteous
Turn rough meeting notes into a tidy action list
Brainstorm ten names for the spring tenant newsletter
Summarize a new state rule on security deposits for the owner
Pull a statistic on local rent increases for a board memo
Add up late fees across a 200-row spreadsheet
Paste tenant names and bank details into a free chatbot
Decide which rental applicant is approved
labs.tip: Drafting and reformatting are safe starting points. Facts and math need checking. Private data and decisions about people need policy and a human.

labs.title: Spot the AI myths
labs.intro: A coworker explains AI assistants at lunch. Tap every statement you should challenge.
segments: An assistant like ChatGPT or Claude writes by predicting the next piece of text.
It learned from a huge amount of writing, and that training stops at a cutoff date.
So when it gives you a source, it has looked it up in its database and the source is real.
Models generate plausible text; sources can be invented and must be checked.
Long chats are fine because it remembers everything you ever typed, forever.
The context window is limited, and early details can drop out of long chats.
Its limits are counted in tokens, which are small chunks of text.
The paid version doesn't make mistakes, so you can skip the review.
Paid plans raise limits and model quality, but every plan can still hallucinate.
I check what our employer has approved before I use a tool for work.
It's a private tool, so pasting client records in is safe by default.
Check data settings, company policy and privacy rules before pasting sensitive data.
labs.tip: Four ideas explain most myths: prediction, training cutoff, context limits, and your duty to review.

plaibox.title: Simulation: your first week with an AI assistant
plaibox.intro: You are the operations lead at a 20-person insurance agency in Kansas City. Scoring: 2 = best practice, 1 = partial, 0 = risky.
plaibox.win: Solid start. You tested before trusting, verified what mattered and protected client information.
plaibox.lose: Revisit the 3 Commandments: try the tool yourself, review every output, and keep private data and people decisions safe.

steps.s: The owner asks you to 'get the team using AI.' What is your first move?
o: Email everyone a link and tell them to start using it today
Nobody knows the tool's limits yet, including you.
Use it yourself on a few low-stakes tasks for a week
Investigate and understand before you apply it across the team.
Read reviews for a month before opening any of the tools
Research helps, but hands-on use teaches far more, far sooner.

steps.s: Which assistant should you try first?
o: The one a popular tech blog ranked number one this month
It may be fine, but rankings shift and fit matters more.
A personal account, so the agency's IT rules don't apply
Working around policy puts client data and your job at risk.
One the agency permits that fits the software you use
Approval and fit with your daily tools beat any ranking.

steps.s: The assistant drafts a client letter and states a specific state filing deadline.
o: Confirm the deadline on the state regulator's website
Dates and rules given from memory are prime hallucination territory.
Send it, since the letter reads clearly and professionally
Polished wording says nothing about whether the date is right.
Ask the assistant to double-check its own deadline
It can repeat the same error; go to the original source.

steps.s: A colleague wants to paste a client's claim file, with health details, into a free chatbot.
o: Fine, as long as the chat is deleted when they finish
Deleting a chat doesn't settle how the data was handled.
Ban the team from using AI on any client work at all
Safe, but it throws away low-risk uses such as generic drafting.
Remove identifying details and check the agency's policy
Minimize data and confirm the rules before anything is pasted.

modules.t: Class 2 — Prompting that works: the CLEAR framework
modules.d: Learn to turn vague requests into specific prompts with the five CLEAR elements, then refine results through examples, reference text and follow-up questions.
modules.body:
Why prompting is the skill that pays off first

In Class 1 you saw that an assistant predicts a plausible response to whatever you type. A vague request gets the most average answer on the internet. A specific request gets something you can use. This class gives you a repeatable way to be specific, called CLEAR, plus the conversational habits that turn a decent first draft into a finished one.

Class agenda (90 minutes)

  • 0:00-0:10 Homework debrief: what worked and what you had to correct
  • 0:10-0:20 Weak vs strong prompts, side by side
  • 0:20-0:45 The five CLEAR elements and a worked before/after
  • 0:45-1:00 Advanced moves: context, reference text, examples, iterating, evaluating
  • 1:00-1:20 Labs: build a CLEAR prompt and let the AI interview you
  • 1:20-1:30 Start your prompt library, then homework

Weak vs strong prompts

A weak prompt leaves the assistant guessing who is writing, to whom, and why. Compare:

  • Weak: "Write a job posting for a receptionist."
  • Strong: "Act as an HR generalist at a family dental office in Tucson. Write a 200-word job posting for a full-time receptionist, in a welcoming tone, for applicants with front-desk experience who may not have worked in health care. Include the hours (Monday to Thursday, 7:30 to 4:30) and how to apply. Use short paragraphs and a bulleted list of duties."

The strong version is longer, and every sentence removes a guess.

The five CLEAR elements

Team21's CLEAR checklist names five things a good prompt tells the assistant.

  1. Persona. The role you want it to take: "Act as an experienced bookkeeper for small restaurants." A role steers vocabulary and priorities. It does not make the facts more reliable.
  2. Tone. How it should sound: warm, formal, firm but friendly, plain and direct.
  3. Format. The shape of the output: an email with a subject line, a table, five bullets, a one-page memo, a word limit.
  4. Details. The facts only you know: dates, names of programs, amounts, constraints, what to leave out.
  5. Target audience. Who will read it and what they already know: new hires, a board of directors, parents, customers reading on a phone.
Key takeaway: you rarely need all five in full. Details and Target audience do the most work, so start there if you are short on time.

Worked example: before and after

Luis coordinates volunteers at a food bank in Minneapolis and has to announce a shift change.

Before: "Write a message to volunteers about the schedule." The result is a cheerful, empty note with placeholder times.

After:

  • Persona: "Act as a volunteer coordinator at a community food bank."
  • Tone: "Warm, appreciative and direct."
  • Format: "An email with a subject line, three short paragraphs, and a bulleted list of the new times."
  • Details: "Starting Saturday, May 3, the morning shift runs 9:00 a.m. to noon (it was 8:00 to 11:00). Volunteers enter through the Pine Street warehouse door. Anyone who can't make the new time should reply by Wednesday."
  • Target audience: "About 40 volunteers, many of them retirees and high school students, who mostly read email on their phones."

The second draft has the right date, door and deadline, and it reads well on a small screen. Luis still checks every detail against his schedule before sending, because Commandment 2 applies to good prompts too.

Advanced moves: Context, Reference, Iterate, Evaluate

  • Context. Say why you need this and what happened before: "Two volunteers quit last month over scheduling confusion, so clarity matters most."
  • Reference. Paste the source material and tell the assistant to work from it: "Answer using only the policy below. If the policy doesn't cover it, say so." This reduces invented answers, though it does not eliminate them.
  • Iterate. Treat the first answer as a draft. Stay in the same conversation and give specific feedback: "Shorter. Cut the second paragraph. Make the subject line a plain statement." Three quick rounds usually beat one giant prompt.
  • Evaluate. Before you use the result, check facts and numbers against your own records, read it as the recipient would, and ask the assistant to critique its own draft.

Examples, and letting the AI interview you

Show an example. If you want your organization's voice, paste one or two past pieces and say "match this style." Examples steer better than adjectives. Remove names and confidential details first.

Ask it to ask you. When you are unsure what to include, end with: "Before you start, ask me up to five questions that would improve the result." The assistant becomes an interviewer, and its questions often surface details you would have forgotten.

A starter prompt library for work

Save prompts that work, with [brackets] for the parts that change. Six to begin with:

  • Email reply: "Act as a [role]. Draft a reply to the email below in a [tone] tone, under [number] words. My key points: [points]. Email: [paste]"
  • Meeting summary: "Summarize these notes for [audience] as decisions, action items with owners and dates, and open questions. Use only what is in the notes. Notes: [paste]"
  • Explain it: "Explain [topic] to a [role] with no background in it. Use one everyday example and note what people commonly get wrong."
  • Critique: "Review my draft as a skeptical [reader]. List the three weakest points and a fix for each. Do not rewrite it yet. Draft: [paste]"
  • Plan: "I need to [goal] by [date]. Ask me up to five questions first, then give me a plan as a table with owner and deadline columns."
  • Rewrite for a reader: "Rewrite the text below for [audience] at a [grade] reading level. Keep every fact the same. Text: [paste]"
🧪 Interactive Lab — try it now

Help me write a strong prompt. My task is: [describe a real work task, with no confidential details]. Interview me one question at a time about the Persona, Tone, Format, Details and Target audience. After my fifth answer, write the finished prompt for me to copy, then run it and show me the result.

🧪 Interactive Lab — try it now

Act as an experienced [your role]. I need a [type of document] for [audience]. Tone: [tone]. Format: [format and length]. Details: [facts, dates and limits]. Before you write anything, ask me up to five questions that would improve the result. After the draft, list anything in it that I should verify.

Homework: write CLEAR prompts for three real tasks, iterate each at least twice, and save the best one in your library.

📚 Glossary

  • Prompt: the instruction, question or material you give an AI assistant.
  • CLEAR: Team21's checklist of Persona, Tone, Format, Details and Target audience.
  • Persona: the role you ask the assistant to take.
  • Reference text: source material you paste in for the assistant to work from.
  • Few-shot prompting: including a few examples of the output you want.
  • Iteration: improving a result through follow-up messages in the same conversation.
  • Prompt library: your saved collection of reusable prompts with placeholders.

📖 References

  • OpenAI. "Prompt engineering" guide, OpenAI platform documentation.
  • Anthropic. "Prompt engineering overview," Claude documentation.
  • Google. "Prompting guide 101" for Gemini in Google Workspace.
  • Microsoft Support. "Learn about Copilot prompts."
  • Mollick, E. (2024). Co-Intelligence: Living and Working with AI. Portfolio.

quiz.q: Tasha, an office manager in Raleigh, types "write a job posting" and gets a bland, generic result that fits no real position. Which change will improve the next attempt the most?
opts: Retype the same request in capital letters to show urgency
Add the role, hours, tone, length and who the applicants are
Open a different assistant and enter the same short request
Ask for a much longer posting so more ground gets covered
quiz.x: Specific details and audience remove the guesses that cause generic output. A different assistant given the same vague request will produce the same kind of average answer.

quiz.q: Omar starts a prompt with "Act as an experienced HR generalist at a mid-size Canadian manufacturer." What can he reasonably expect that opening line to accomplish?
opts: It steers the vocabulary and the priorities of the response
It confirms that the legal points in the answer are accurate
It gives the assistant access to Canadian employment law files
It lets the assistant skip any follow-up questions he asks
quiz.x: A persona shapes focus and wording, which is useful. It does not verify legal accuracy, so Omar still has to check any claims about employment rules.

quiz.q: A landscaping company in Phoenix asks an assistant for a past-due notice to a ten-year customer. The draft is accurate, yet it sounds cold and threatening. What is the best next message?
opts: "Make this notice much better and more professional."
"Start over and write a past-due notice for a customer."
"Rewrite it firm but friendly; we value this relationship."
"Add more details about our late fees and legal options."
quiz.x: Naming the tone and the reason gives the assistant a clear target for the rewrite. "Make it better" leaves it guessing what better means to the sender.

quiz.q: A program director in Ottawa must brief her executive director, who has about 30 seconds to read each update. The assistant returns six dense paragraphs. Which element was missing from her prompt?
opts: Format, such as a two-line summary and three bullets
Tone, since the paragraphs came out too formal in style
Details, since the figures needed more decimal places
Persona, since no job title was given to the assistant
quiz.x: The content was fine and the shape was wrong, so a format instruction fixes it. Changing tone would still leave six paragraphs the reader has no time for.

quiz.q: A nurse educator in Cleveland asks for a handout on managing blood pressure at home. The draft is correct but full of clinical terms her patients will not know. What should she add?
opts: A request to add citations from recent clinical journals
A request for a longer handout with more medical background
A persona line asking the assistant to act as a cardiologist
A note on who the readers are and the reading level they need
quiz.x: Describing the readers lets the assistant choose plain words and useful examples. A cardiologist persona would likely push the language further toward clinical terms.

quiz.q: Ben, a sales rep in Edmonton, gets a proposal draft that is about 70 percent right: good structure, an opening that runs long, and one section he does not need. What should he do?
opts: Open a new chat and retype the original prompt word for word
Reply in the same chat with the specific changes he wants made
Accept the draft as written, since most of it is already usable
Switch to another assistant and compare the two full drafts
quiz.x: Iterating in the same conversation keeps the context and fixes only what is off. A fresh chat with the same prompt throws away the good 70 percent and may repeat the flaws.

quiz.q: A credit union in Portland wants its member newsletter drafted in its usual friendly, plainspoken voice. Describing that voice with adjectives has not worked. What should the writer try next?
opts: Add five more adjectives describing the voice in greater depth
Request three versions and pick whichever one sounds closest
Ask the assistant to guess the voice from the credit union's name
Paste two past newsletters and ask it to match their style
quiz.x: Examples show the voice directly, which steers better than description. More adjectives repeat the approach that has already failed to capture the style.

quiz.q: An HR assistant in Boston needs to answer an employee's question about bereavement leave and wants the reply to reflect her company's actual policy. Which prompt approach is the most dependable?
opts: Ask the assistant to recall the policy from the company's website
Paste the policy and ask for an answer drawn from that text alone
Ask what bereavement leave policies are typical in Massachusetts
Tell the assistant the company is generous and let it fill in the rest
quiz.x: Reference text grounds the answer in the real policy and reduces invented details. Typical state practices may differ from what this company actually offers.

quiz.q: Carla, who runs a bookkeeping practice in Regina, wants help planning a client appreciation event but is not sure what information the assistant needs from her. What is a smart way to begin?
opts: Ask the assistant to pose a few questions before it drafts a plan
Request a generic event plan and correct it line by line afterward
Wait to use the assistant until she has decided all the details
Paste her full client list so the assistant has every detail
quiz.x: Letting the assistant interview her surfaces budget, date and guest details quickly. Pasting a client list exposes private information the task does not need.

quiz.q: An assistant drafts a renewal proposal for a Chicago IT firm, including three price figures and a contract end date. The account manager likes how it reads. What does the Evaluate step call for?
opts: Send it right away while the client is still expecting it
Run the same prompt again and send whichever draft is longer
Check the figures and date against the firm's own records
Ask the assistant to make the proposal sound more confident
quiz.x: Evaluating means confirming facts and numbers at the source before anything goes out. Good wording is no evidence that the prices or the date are correct.

facts.t: Persona, Tone, Format, Details, Target audience.
facts.more: These are the five CLEAR elements taught at Team21. Details and Target audience usually do the most to lift a weak prompt.

modules.t: Class 3 — Trust, but verify: accuracy, privacy and safe use at work
modules.d: Learn why AI gets things wrong, a 4-step routine to verify its output, and what to keep out of AI tools so your work stays accurate, private and fair.
modules.body:
Why this class matters

You have seen what an AI assistant can do. This class covers what it gets wrong and how a careful professional uses it anyway. Treat its output the way you would treat a new hire's first draft: assume good effort, check the facts, and keep confidential material where it belongs. That is Commandment 2 (review for hallucinations, keep a human in the loop) and Commandment 3 (do no harm) turned into daily habits.

Class agenda (90 minutes)

  • 0:00 to 0:10 Welcome and homework review: one prompt that worked, one that did not
  • 0:10 to 0:25 Hallucinations: what they are and why they happen
  • 0:25 to 0:45 The 4-step verification routine, sources and citations, Lab 1
  • 0:45 to 1:00 What never to paste, privacy basics, workplace AI policies
  • 1:00 to 1:15 Bias and disclosure, Lab 2
  • 1:15 to 1:30 Worked example debrief, quiz, homework

Hallucinations: fluent, confident and wrong

A hallucination is output that sounds right and is false or invented: a court case that does not exist, a statistic with no source, a quote nobody said. It happens because a language model writes the most plausible next words based on patterns in its training data. Unless it is connected to search or to your documents, it is not looking anything up, and even a connected tool can misread a page. Risk rises when:

  • the topic is recent, local or niche (your county's permit rules, last month's news);
  • you ask for specifics such as citations, numbers, dates, quotes or links;
  • your question assumes something false, and the model plays along;
  • the document is long and the model fills gaps instead of saying "not stated."

The consequences are real. In 2023 a federal judge in New York sanctioned lawyers who filed a brief citing cases a chatbot had invented (Mata v. Avianca). In 2024 a British Columbia tribunal held Air Canada responsible for wrong information its website chatbot gave a customer (Moffatt v. Air Canada). In both, the people who used the output owned it.

Key takeaway: Fluency is not evidence. The more specific and checkable a claim is, the more it needs checking.

The 4-step verification routine

  1. Flag every checkable claim: names, numbers, dates, quotes, citations, and anything legal, medical or financial.
  2. Trace each one to a source. Ask the assistant where it came from, then open the source yourself.
  3. Cross-check against an independent, authoritative source such as a government agency, the original study or your own records.
  4. Own the result: fix it, cut it or send it to an expert, and note what you verified.

Scale the effort to the stakes. A brainstorm list needs a glance. Anything that goes to a client, a regulator or the public, or that concerns a named person, gets all four steps.

Checking sources and citations

  • Links: open each one. Does the page exist, and does it say what the assistant claims?
  • Citations: search the title and authors in Google Scholar, a library database or the publisher's site. Invented citations often pair real authors with titles they did not write.
  • Quotes: search the exact phrase in quotation marks.
  • Numbers: find the original (the Bureau of Labor Statistics, Statistics Canada, a company filing) and confirm the year and the unit.

Web-connected assistants show their sources, which helps, yet they can still summarize a page inaccurately. Asking "are you sure?" does not count as verification: the tool may defend a wrong answer or abandon a right one.

🧪 Interactive Lab — try it now

Give me five statistics about remote work in the United States and Canada, with a named source and year for each. Then rank the five from most to least certain, and for each one tell me exactly how I could verify it myself, including where to look.

Pick two of the five and run all four steps. Report what held up.

Worked example: the statistic that was not there

Dana coordinates programs at a literacy nonprofit in Columbus, Ohio. She asks an assistant to draft a paragraph for a funder report, and the draft says a named university study found that tutoring raised reading scores by 31 percent. (This example is illustrative.)

  1. Flag: the percentage and the named study.
  2. Trace: she asks for the source. The assistant supplies a title and a link, and the link opens an error page.
  3. Cross-check: she searches the title in Google Scholar and on the university's site and finds nothing.
  4. Own: she cuts the sentence and uses her program's own results, confirmed by her director.

Total time: about eight minutes, far less than a correction letter to a funder would take.

What never to paste into a consumer AI tool

A consumer tool is a free or personal account your employer has not approved. Depending on the product and your settings, chats may be stored, reviewed by staff or used to improve models. Those settings change, so check the provider's current data controls. Keep these out:

  • Social Security or Social Insurance numbers, license and passport numbers;
  • health details about patients, clients or coworkers;
  • student records and grades;
  • bank, payroll and card numbers, passwords and access keys;
  • client files, contracts under NDA, unreleased financials, source code;
  • HR matters such as reviews, complaints and investigations.

Safer options: replace identifiers with placeholders ("Client A"), describe the situation in general terms, or use a tool your employer has approved under a business agreement.

Privacy basics and workplace AI policies

This is general education, not legal advice. The United States has no single comprehensive federal privacy law, so rules vary by sector and by state. HIPAA generally covers health plans, providers and their business associates. FERPA protects student education records at schools that receive federal education funding. Some states, including California, have their own consumer privacy laws. In Canada, PIPEDA generally applies to private-sector organizations handling personal information in commercial activity, and Quebec, Alberta and British Columbia have their own private-sector laws. Whether a particular use is allowed depends on your role, your contracts and the tool.

So ask before you act. Find your employer's AI policy through IT, HR or compliance. Most policies name the approved tools, the kinds of data allowed, review requirements and disclosure rules. If there is no policy, ask your manager in writing and apply the strictest reasonable default.

Bias and disclosure

Models learn from human writing, so they can repeat its stereotypes: who is described as a "leader," whose résumé looks "polished." The risk is highest in hiring, performance reviews, lending, admissions and discipline. Do not let AI decide about people by itself. Ask it to list its assumptions, test a prompt by swapping names or genders, and review results against written criteria.

On disclosure, follow your employer, client, school or court rules first. A reasonable default is to disclose when AI materially shaped the work and a reader would feel misled to learn it later. One line is enough: "Drafted with AI assistance; reviewed and verified by [name]." Either way, you remain accountable.

🧪 Interactive Lab — try it now

Act as a careful privacy reviewer. I will paste a draft prompt I plan to send to an AI tool. Do not answer the prompt. List any personal, confidential or regulated details in it, explain the risk of each in one line, then rewrite the prompt with those details removed or replaced by placeholders such as [Client A]. My draft prompt: [paste a made-up example here, not real data]

Commandments 2 and 3 in practice: verify before you rely, protect people before you paste, and put your name on work you would defend.

📚 Glossary

  • Hallucination: AI output that sounds plausible and is false or invented.
  • Knowledge cutoff: the date after which a model has no training data.
  • Human in the loop: a person reviews and approves AI output before it is used.
  • Personal information: data that identifies a person, alone or combined with other data.
  • De-identification: removing or replacing details that point to a specific person.
  • Consumer AI tool: a free or personal account not covered by your employer's agreement.
  • Bias: a systematic skew in output that treats groups of people unfairly.
  • Disclosure: telling readers that AI helped produce the work.

📖 References

  • National Institute of Standards and Technology (2023). AI Risk Management Framework (AI RMF 1.0).
  • Mata v. Avianca, Inc., U.S. District Court, Southern District of New York (2023), sanctions order.
  • Moffatt v. Air Canada, 2024 BCCRT 149 (British Columbia Civil Resolution Tribunal).
  • U.S. Department of Health and Human Services. HIPAA Privacy Rule guidance (hhs.gov/hipaa).
  • U.S. Department of Education. FERPA guidance (studentprivacy.ed.gov).
  • Office of the Privacy Commissioner of Canada. PIPEDA overview and generative AI principles (priv.gc.ca).
  • Your AI provider's current privacy and data-control pages (these change often; check them directly).

quiz.q: A paralegal in Chicago asks a chatbot for case law to support a motion and receives three citations with realistic party names and docket numbers. What should she do first?
opts: Look up each case in a legal database before using it
Ask the chatbot to confirm that the cases are real
Use the ones that have the most detailed docket numbers listed
Add a footnote saying an AI tool found the cases
quiz.x: Checking a legal database traces each claim to an independent source. Asking the chatbot to confirm is the runner-up, but the same tool that invented a case can also 'confirm' it.

quiz.q: An HR manager in Toronto wonders why an assistant invented a company policy clause that sounded official. Which explanation best fits how these tools actually work?
opts: The model ran out of memory and filled the gap with random text instead
The model was trained to mislead users who ask vague questions
The model predicts plausible wording and has no built-in fact check
The model searched the web and copied a mistaken page it found
quiz.x: Language models generate likely next words, so official-sounding text can be invented. A copied web error is possible with search tools, but it does not explain a clause that exists nowhere.

quiz.q: A marketing analyst in Denver receives an AI-drafted report containing a market-size figure, a CEO quote and two links. Following the class routine, which sequence is correct?
opts: Own the result, cross-check, trace the sources, then flag the claims
Flag the claims, trace sources, cross-check, then own the result
Cross-check, flag the claims, own the result, then trace the sources
Trace sources, own the result, flag the claims, then cross-check them
quiz.x: You cannot trace what you have not flagged, and you should not sign off until an independent check is done. Starting with tracing skips the step that tells you which claims matter.

quiz.q: A nurse manager at a clinic in Phoenix wants help rewording a discharge summary, and a free personal chatbot account is already open in her browser. What is the best move?
opts: Paste it in, then delete the chat as soon as she has finished the letter
Turn on private browsing mode before pasting the summary
Paste it in, since the summary describes a routine case
Remove identifying details or use a tool the clinic approved
quiz.x: De-identifying or using an approved tool keeps patient information out of an unapproved service. Deleting the chat afterward is the runner-up, but the data has already left the clinic's control.

quiz.q: A teacher in Calgary plans to paste a class list with student names and grades into an AI tool to draft report-card comments. Which step should come before anything else?
opts: Ask the AI tool whether it keeps student information
Read a recent tech blog review of the tool's privacy features
Shorten the list so it shows first names and grades
Check the school board's policy and approved tools list
quiz.x: The board's policy decides what is allowed with student records. Trimming to first names reduces exposure a little, yet it is still identifiable student data in a tool nobody has approved.

quiz.q: An operations lead at a 40-person firm in Atlanta discovers there is no written AI policy. A coworker says that means anything goes. What is the most responsible response?
opts: Agree, because rules apply once a formal policy has been published
Follow what the tool's marketing page says about safety
Ask a manager in writing and keep sensitive data out for now
Stop using AI tools at work until the law becomes clearer
quiz.x: Asking in writing creates a record and a strict default protects people meanwhile. Stopping all use is safe but unnecessary, since low-risk tasks with no sensitive data can continue.

quiz.q: A small-business owner in Oregon asks a web-connected assistant about a new state overtime rule and gets an answer with four source links. What do those links tell her?
opts: That the rule is current as of the day she asked about it
Where to start checking, since summaries can misstate a source
That the assistant quoted each page word for word in its reply
That the answer has been reviewed by the listed publishers
quiz.x: Links make tracing faster, but the summary can still be wrong, so she must read them. Assuming the rule is current is tempting, yet a linked page may be outdated or about another state.

quiz.q: A recruiter in Minneapolis uses AI to summarize 60 résumés and notices that candidates with career gaps receive noticeably weaker summaries. What is the best next step?
opts: Review those files herself and test the prompt for skewed patterns
Switch to a different chatbot and rerun the same sixty résumés
Ask the tool to rank the candidates so the gaps matter less to her
Keep the summaries, since the tool treats each résumé the same way
quiz.x: Human review plus testing addresses both the affected candidates and the cause. Switching chatbots is the runner-up, but a new tool can carry the same bias and nobody has checked.

quiz.q: A consultant in Vancouver used AI to draft about half of a client report, then verified and edited it. The contract is silent on AI. Which approach best fits class guidance?
opts: Add a short note that AI assisted and that he reviewed the work
List the AI tool as a co-author on the report's title page
Say nothing, because he edited the draft himself before it went out
Tell the client the AI is responsible for any errors found
quiz.x: AI materially shaped the report, so a brief note avoids misleading the client while he stays accountable. Silence may be permitted, but it risks trust if the client learns of it later.

quiz.q: A grant writer in Halifax asks an assistant 'are you sure?' about a statistic. It apologizes and supplies a different number. What should she conclude from this exchange?
opts: The second number is right because the tool corrected itself
Neither number is verified until she finds the original source
The first number was right and the tool gave in to pressure
The tool is broken and should be reported to her IT help desk today
quiz.x: A model can change its answer under pushback whether or not it was wrong, so only a source settles it. Trusting the 'corrected' number is the runner-up error because it feels like progress.

plaibox.title: Simulation: the board report due at 4 p.m.
plaibox.intro: You are an analyst at a credit union in Ohio, finishing a board report with AI help. Scoring: 2 = best practice, 1 = partial, 0 = risky.
plaibox.win: Strong judgment. You verified what mattered, protected member data and stayed accountable for the report.
plaibox.lose: Revisit the routine: Flag, Trace, Cross-check, Own, and keep regulated data out of unapproved tools.

steps.s: The AI draft says 'industry surveys show 62% of members prefer mobile banking.' You have 40 minutes.
o: Keep it; the number sounds about right for the industry today
Plausible is not verified. A board may act on this number.
Ask for the source, open it and confirm the figure
Trace and cross-check: the heart of the routine.
Soften it to 'most members' and leave out the source
Lower risk, but still an unsupported claim in a board report.

steps.s: The assistant names a survey and gives a link. The link opens a page that does not mention the figure.
o: Cite the survey anyway, since the link at least exists
A real link that does not support the claim is still a false citation.
Ask the assistant again until it offers another link
It may help, but repeated asking can produce more invented sources.
Cut the claim or use your own member data instead
If you cannot verify it, fix or cut. Your own records are the strongest source.

steps.s: A colleague suggests pasting the member complaint log, with names and account numbers, into a free chatbot to find themes.
o: Use the approved tool, or strip identifiers first
Protects members and follows policy while still getting the analysis.
Paste it and delete the conversation right afterward
The data has already left your control; deletion may not undo that.
Paste the log with names removed but account numbers kept
Better, but account numbers still identify members.

steps.s: The report is ready. AI drafted two sections that you verified and edited. Your credit union's policy asks for disclosure.
o: Skip the note, since you checked every line yourself
The policy asks for disclosure regardless of how well you checked.
Add a line: AI-assisted, reviewed and verified by you
Honest, brief, and it keeps accountability with a named person.
Mention it verbally if a board member happens to ask
Better than silence, but the policy calls for it up front.

modules.t: Class 4 — AI for everyday work: writing, email, meetings and research
modules.d: Put AI to work on drafting, email, meeting notes, long documents and cited research, measure the time it really saves, and stay the editor of everything you send.
modules.body:
From safe to useful

Class 3 gave you guardrails. This class puts AI to work on the four things that fill most office days: writing, email, meetings and research. One rule runs through all of it: AI drafts, you edit and decide. You supply the facts, the judgment and the final say.

Class agenda (90 minutes)

  • 0:00 to 0:10 Welcome and homework review: what you verified last week
  • 0:10 to 0:30 Drafting and editing in your own voice, worked example
  • 0:30 to 0:45 Email triage and replies, Lab 1
  • 0:45 to 1:00 Meeting notes, action items and long-document summaries
  • 1:00 to 1:15 Research with cited sources, Lab 2
  • 1:15 to 1:30 Time audit setup, quiz, homework

Drafting and editing in your own voice

Left alone, AI writes in a smooth, generic voice that readers increasingly recognize. The fix is to teach it yours:

  1. Paste two or three non-confidential samples of your own writing.
  2. Ask: "Describe my writing style in five bullet points."
  3. Save that description as a reusable voice note and paste it at the top of future requests.

Then use the CLEAR elements from Class 2: Persona, Tone, Format, Details and Target audience. There are two working modes. In draft mode you give bullet points and the facts, and the AI writes sentences. In edit mode you write first and ask for a tighter version, with a list of what changed and why. Edit mode keeps more of you in the result.

Before anything goes out, run the editor's check: Are the facts right? Does it sound like me? Would I say this out loud? What can I cut?

Worked example: one email, two prompts

Maya manages the office at a dental practice in Raleigh, North Carolina. She needs to tell staff about a new scheduling system.

Before: "Write an email about the new scheduling system." The result is long, opens with "We are thrilled to announce," and invents a training date.

After: "You are an office manager writing to 14 dental staff (Persona, Target audience). Friendly and direct, no corporate language (Tone). Under 150 words with a short bulleted list (Format). Details: the new system goes live Monday, June 8; training is Thursday at 12:30 in the break room, lunch provided; old appointment books are retired Friday. If a detail is missing, ask me instead of guessing."

Maya then edits: she confirms both dates against her calendar, cuts one filler sentence and adds a line thanking the front desk. Total time is about six minutes, where she used to spend twenty.

Key takeaway: Specific facts in, usable draft out. Telling the AI to ask instead of guess removes most invented details.

Email triage and replies

Many mail and office suites now include assistants. Features and prices vary by plan and change often, so check what your organization has switched on, and use approved tools for work mail.

  • Triage: sort messages into three piles: reply today, delegate or schedule, and FYI.
  • Long threads: ask who is asking for what, what has been decided, what is still open, and what is needed from you.
  • Replies: you make the decision and list the points. The AI handles the wording.
  • Before sending: check names, dates, amounts, attachments and tone. Do not let a tool send on your behalf without review.
🧪 Interactive Lab — try it now

Below is an email thread with names and private details removed. Summarize it in four parts: (1) who is asking for what, (2) decisions already made, (3) open questions, (4) what is needed from me and by when. Then draft a reply of under 120 words, in a friendly and direct tone, that says the following: [your decision and key points]. If anything is unclear, ask me before drafting. Thread: [paste here]

Meeting notes and action items

Before: ask AI to turn your goals into a timed agenda. During: several meeting platforms offer transcription and AI summaries on some plans. Tell participants before you record. Recording and consent rules differ across states and provinces, and some require everyone's agreement, so follow your employer's policy. After: have the AI turn the transcript or your notes into decisions, action items with an owner and a due date, and open questions.

Then check the output against what you remember. AI notes can attribute a comment to the wrong speaker or record a suggestion as a decision. Send the corrected notes within a day while memories are fresh.

Summarizing long documents

  • Give the summary a purpose: "Summarize for a director deciding whether to renew this contract."
  • Ask for a page or section reference beside each point so you can spot-check.
  • Ask what the summary left out and what a skeptical reader would question.
  • Spot-check at least three points against the original. Very long files may be read unevenly.

A summary helps you decide what to read closely. For a contract or anything you will sign, it does not replace reading.

Research with cited sources

Web-connected assistants search the internet and list their sources. That makes them far more useful for current questions than a model working from memory, and capabilities differ by product and plan. A strong research prompt states the question, the scope (place and date range), a preference for primary sources such as government agencies and peer-reviewed studies, and an output format that makes checking easy.

🧪 Interactive Lab — try it now

Research this question using web search: [your question]. Scope: United States and Canada, sources from the last two years. Prefer primary sources such as government agencies, standards bodies and peer-reviewed studies. Return a table with four columns: Claim, Source, Date published, Link. After the table, note where sources disagree and which claims you are least confident about.

Then apply the Class 3 routine. Open at least two of the links and confirm each page says what the table claims.

Your before/after time audit

Pick three tasks you repeat every week. For each, record the minutes it takes by hand, the minutes with AI, the minutes you spend reviewing and fixing, and whether quality is the same, better or worse. Keep AI where the net saving is real and quality holds. Drop it where review eats the gain.

Research supports measuring for yourself. In a 2023 study in Science, professionals using a chatbot for writing tasks finished about 40 percent faster, with higher-rated quality. A Harvard Business School study of consultants found that AI helped on tasks suited to it and hurt accuracy on a task outside its strengths. Your tasks will fall on both sides of that line.

AI can hand you a first draft in seconds. The facts, the judgment and the signature are still yours.

📚 Glossary

  • Voice note: a short description of your writing style that you reuse in prompts.
  • Draft mode / edit mode: AI writes from your points, or AI tightens what you wrote.
  • Triage: sorting incoming items by urgency and by who should handle them.
  • Action item: a task with a named owner and a due date.
  • Transcript: a written record of what was said in a meeting.
  • Web-connected assistant: an AI tool that searches the internet and cites sources.
  • Primary source: the original document, dataset or study behind a claim.
  • Time audit: a before/after record of how long tasks take, including review.

📖 References

  • Noy, S., and Zhang, W. (2023). Experimental evidence on the productivity effects of generative artificial intelligence. Science, 381(6654).
  • Brynjolfsson, E., Li, D., and Raymond, L. (2023). Generative AI at Work. NBER Working Paper 31161.
  • Dell'Acqua, F., et al. (2023). Navigating the Jagged Technological Frontier. Harvard Business School Working Paper 24-013.
  • McKinsey Global Institute (2012). The social economy: Unlocking value and productivity through social technologies.
  • Mollick, E. (2024). Co-Intelligence: Living and Working with AI. Portfolio.
  • Your mail, meeting and AI providers' current help pages for features, pricing and recording settings (these change often).

quiz.q: A communications coordinator in Boston finds that her AI drafts sound stiff and generic compared with the newsletters she normally writes. Which step would help most?
opts: Switch to a paid plan, since paid models write in a much warmer tone
Ask the tool to write a longer draft with more adjectives in it
Tell the tool to sound human and to avoid robotic phrases

quiz.x: Real samples give the model a concrete pattern to follow. 'Sound human' is the runner-up, but a vague instruction gives the tool nothing specific about her particular voice.

quiz.q: An office manager in Winnipeg returns from vacation to 180 unread emails and has an employer-approved assistant built into her mail app. What is the best first use of it?
opts: Have it delete messages older than a week to clear space
Ask it to draft one apology to send to all of her contacts at once

Have it send short replies to every message in the inbox
quiz.x: Triage shows her what needs attention before anything is sent. Bulk replies look efficient, but they commit her to answers she has not read or decided on.

quiz.q: A project lead in Seattle must answer a vendor who wants a two-week extension. He has already decided to offer one week. How should he use an AI assistant here?
opts: Ask it whether the vendor deserves the full extension
Let it reply automatically using his past messages
Give it his decision and key points, then edit the wording
Paste the contract and have it choose the best terms
quiz.x: He keeps the decision and delegates the phrasing, then reviews it. Asking the AI what the vendor deserves hands over a judgment that depends on context it does not have.

quiz.q: After a budget meeting in Ottawa, the AI notetaker's summary says the team 'decided to cut travel by 15 percent.' A manager remembers it as a suggestion. What should she do?
opts: Delete the summary and stop sending notes after budget meetings
Check the transcript or attendees, then correct it before sending
Forward it and let attendees reply if they notice a problem
Send the summary as written, since the tool heard the full meeting
quiz.x: AI notes can turn a suggestion into a decision, so she verifies and fixes it. Forwarding it for others to catch is the runner-up, but an uncorrected 'decision' may be acted on first.

quiz.q: A team lead in Dallas wants to switch on an AI notetaker for weekly client calls that include participants in several different states. What should come first?
opts: Ask the notetaker vendor whether clients usually mind recording
Record a few calls as a trial and mention it if the notes are good
Turn it on quietly so the conversation stays natural for clients
Check company policy and tell participants it will be recording
quiz.x: Consent rules differ by state and employer policy governs, so check and inform first. A quiet trial is the runner-up idea, and it risks breaking consent rules and client trust.

quiz.q: A nonprofit director in Montreal must brief her board on a 70-page funding agreement and asks an AI tool for a summary. Which request makes that summary easiest to trust?
opts: Ask for section references on each point, then spot-check several
Ask for the summary twice and keep the version that reads better
Ask the tool to rate its own confidence from one to ten per point
Ask for the shortest possible summary so there is less to review
quiz.x: References let her confirm points against the agreement itself. A self-rated confidence score is the runner-up, but the tool's own rating is not evidence that a point is accurate.

quiz.q: A small-business owner in Tampa asks a web-connected assistant about sales tax on online orders and gets a tidy answer with five links. What is the best next step?
opts: Act on the answer, because search-based tools pull live facts
Count the links, since five sources means it is well supported
Open the links, favoring the state revenue agency's own page
Ask a second chatbot and go with whichever answer is repeated
quiz.x: The agency's page is the primary source and settles the question. A second chatbot is the runner-up, but two tools can repeat the same outdated or misread information.

quiz.q: An analyst in Edmonton is writing a research prompt on remote-work trends for a leadership memo. Which addition would most improve the quality of what comes back?
opts: Scope, date range, and a table of claim, source, date and link
A request for as many statistics as the tool is able to produce
A request to make the findings sound confident and persuasive
A note that the memo is urgent and must be done within the hour
quiz.x: Scope and a checkable table focus the search and make verification fast. Asking for many statistics is the runner-up, but volume raises the odds of weak or invented figures.

quiz.q: A bookkeeper in Sacramento times a monthly client summary: 45 minutes by hand, versus 10 minutes with AI plus 30 minutes fixing its errors. What does her time audit suggest?
opts: The errors will fade as the tool learns her clients over time
The task takes 10 minutes now, so AI saves her 35 minutes
The review step can be skipped once the drafts look polished
The net saving is small, so refine the prompt or drop this use
quiz.x: Counting review time, she saves 5 minutes, which may not be worth it yet. The 35-minute claim is the common mistake: it leaves out the 30 minutes of fixing that the audit exists to capture.

quiz.q: A school administrator in Buffalo has AI draft a parent letter about a schedule change. The draft is polished, but one date is wrong. Who is accountable if it goes out?
opts: The AI vendor, since its tool produced the wrong date
The administrator, since she reviews and sends it
The parents, since they can call to confirm the date
The IT office, since it approved the tool for staff
quiz.x: The person who sends the message owns it; that is the human-editor rule. The vendor is the runner-up answer, but tools are sold with the expectation that users check the output.

facts.t: Less time on professional writing tasks with a chatbot, in one experiment.
facts.more: Noy and Zhang found that college-educated professionals finished writing tasks about 40% faster and evaluators rated the output higher. Results on your tasks may differ.

facts.t: Average productivity gain for customer-support agents using an AI assistant.
facts.more: The study of more than 5,000 agents found the largest gains among newer and less experienced workers.

facts.t: Share of the workweek knowledge workers spent on email in a 2012 estimate.
facts.more: McKinsey Global Institute estimated that reading and answering email took about 28% of the average interaction worker's week. The figure predates today's AI tools.

facts.t: Consultants in the Harvard-led 'jagged frontier' field experiment.
facts.more: AI improved speed and quality on tasks suited to it, and made consultants less likely to be correct on a task outside its strengths. Knowing which is which takes practice.

Purpose-driven summary with section references
You need current facts on a state rule
Web-connected search with a source table
You are unsure whether AI is saving time
