modules.t: Class 5 — Beyond text: data, documents, images, voice and simple automation
modules.d: Use AI with spreadsheets, PDFs, images and voice, save reusable setups, and sketch a first no-code automation that keeps a human approval step.
modules.body:
So far you have typed questions and read answers. Most AI assistants now accept files, pictures and speech as well, and they can be set up once and reused. This class shows what that makes possible at work, and where the 3 Commandments of AI matter most: investigate before you rely on a feature, review every output with a human in the loop, and do no harm with other people's data.

Features, file limits and prices differ by product and plan, and they change often. Check your own tool's help pages before promising anything to a boss or client.

Class agenda (90 minutes)

  • 0:00-0:10 Warm-up: one task from last week that involved a file, a photo or a meeting
  • 0:10-0:30 Spreadsheets: analyze with AI, then check the math (demo and Lab 1)
  • 0:30-0:45 PDFs and long documents: summaries you can trace to a page
  • 0:45-0:58 Images, voice mode and transcription: uses and limits
  • 0:58-1:12 Reusable setups: saving your context once (Lab 2)
  • 1:12-1:25 Sketch a first automation with a human approval step
  • 1:25-1:30 Recap and homework for the capstone

Spreadsheets: let AI analyze, then check its math

Many assistants can read a CSV or Excel file, describe the columns, find patterns and draw charts. Some run real calculations behind the scenes with a code tool. Others estimate from the text they read, and a language model that estimates can add a column wrong while sounding certain. You often cannot tell which happened, so treat every number as a draft.

Use three quick checks before a figure leaves your desk:

  1. Row count. Ask how many rows it read and compare with your file.
  2. One total. Recalculate a headline number yourself with a SUM or pivot table.
  3. One sample. Pick a single row or category and trace it by hand.

A helpful habit is to ask the assistant for the spreadsheet formula instead of the answer. You paste the formula into Excel or Google Sheets, and the spreadsheet does the arithmetic.

Worked example: the bakery sales export

Sam owns a bakery in Denver and uploads a year of point-of-sale data: 1,460 rows with date, product, quantity and amount. The assistant reports annual sales of $412,300 and names December the top month.

Sam runs the three checks. The assistant says it read 1,460 rows, which matches. A SUM in the spreadsheet returns $418,950, which does not match. Sam asks, "Your total is $6,650 lower than my SUM. Which rows did you leave out and why?" The assistant finds that 38 catering rows stored the amount as text with a dollar sign, so they were skipped. Sam cleans the column, reruns the analysis, and the totals agree. December is still the top month.

The check took about five minutes, and it kept a wrong number out of a loan application.

🧪 Interactive Lab — try it now

Act as a careful data analyst for a small business. I am uploading a spreadsheet of [describe the data, e.g. 12 months of sales]. Step 1: tell me how many rows and columns you read and list the column names. Step 2: flag blanks, duplicates, or numbers stored as text. Step 3: give me three plain-English findings for a non-technical owner. For every number you report, also give the exact Excel or Google Sheets formula I can use to verify it myself. If you estimated instead of calculating, say so.

Key takeaway: AI is quick at finding the story in your data. You remain responsible for the arithmetic. Row count, one total, one sample.

PDFs and long documents

Uploading a contract, policy manual or report and asking questions about it is one of the most useful things a beginner can do. Three limits are worth knowing:

  • Scanned pages may be pictures. If you cannot select the text in a PDF, the tool may not be able to read it without OCR. Some tools apply OCR automatically and some do not.
  • Long files can be read partially. Each tool has a context window. Very long documents may be shortened or searched in pieces, so details in the middle can be missed.
  • Summaries drop nuance. Exceptions, dates and dollar amounts are what a summary tends to lose, and they are what you need most.

Ask for answers with a page or section reference and a short direct quote, then open the document and confirm the two or three points that matter. Think carefully before uploading documents with client, patient or student information. Rules such as HIPAA, FERPA or PIPEDA may apply depending on your role and employer, so follow your organization's policy and use approved tools.

Images, voice and transcription

Image generation is good for concept art, social graphics, slide backgrounds and brainstorming. It is weaker at exact text, accurate logos, charts with real numbers, and consistent details such as hands or a repeated character, though quality keeps improving. Add prices and dates in a design tool afterward. Avoid realistic images of real people without consent, be open about AI-made images where your audience would care, and ask before using them commercially, since copyright questions around AI output are still being worked out.

Voice mode lets you talk with the assistant. It suits rehearsing a hard conversation, thinking aloud on a walk, or language practice. Transcription turns a recorded meeting into text and action items. Expect mistakes with names, numbers, accents and cross-talk, and replay the recording for anything that will be quoted or voted on. Recording consent rules differ across states and provinces, so tell participants and get agreement first.

Reusable setups: save your context once

If you paste the same background into every chat, save it. Most major assistants offer some version of these, under different names and sometimes on paid plans:

  • Custom instructions: standing preferences applied to your chats, such as your role, tone and format.
  • Projects or workspaces: a folder that keeps related chats together with reference files and instructions.
  • Custom assistants (for example custom GPTs or Gems): a purpose-built helper you configure once and may be able to share.

These are the CLEAR elements stored for reuse: Persona, Tone, Format, Details and Target audience, plus Context and Reference files. Keep confidential data out of anything you share, and Iterate and Evaluate the setup after a week of real use.

🧪 Interactive Lab — try it now

Help me write reusable custom instructions for my AI assistant. Interview me first: ask five short questions, one at a time, about my role, my typical audience, the tone I want, the formats I use most, and anything you should avoid. Then write a setup of under 200 words that I can paste into my assistant's custom instructions or project settings. Include one line telling the assistant to say when it is unsure and to ask before assuming facts.

A first automation, with a human approval step

No-code tools such as Zapier, Make and Microsoft Power Automate connect apps with a simple recipe: when this happens, do that. Adding an AI step lets the recipe draft or sort things for you. A sensible first design:

  1. Trigger: a new inquiry arrives through your website form.
  2. AI step: draft a polite reply using your saved template and the customer's question.
  3. Approval: the draft goes to you as an email draft or chat message.
  4. Action: you edit and send it yourself.

The AI saves typing and you keep the judgment. Leave prices, refunds, legal commitments and anything sensitive with a person, and keep the approval step until you have a long record of drafts that needed no changes.

Automate the draft. Keep the decision.

📚 Glossary

  • Multimodal: able to work with more than one kind of input or output, such as text, images, audio and files.
  • CSV: a plain-text spreadsheet format with values separated by commas, readable by nearly every tool.
  • OCR: optical character recognition, which converts a picture of text into text a computer can read.
  • Context window: the amount of text a model can consider at one time.
  • Transcription: converting speech in a recording into written text.
  • Custom instructions: saved preferences an assistant applies to your conversations.
  • Trigger: the event that starts an automation.
  • Human in the loop: a person reviews and approves before an AI output is used or sent.

📖 References

  • National Institute of Standards and Technology, AI Risk Management Framework (AI RMF 1.0), 2023.
  • Official help centers for your assistant (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google Gemini, Microsoft Copilot) for current file, voice and image features; these change often.
  • U.S. Copyright Office, Copyright and Artificial Intelligence report series.
  • U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HIPAA), U.S. Department of Education (FERPA), and Office of the Privacy Commissioner of Canada (PIPEDA) guidance pages.
  • Zapier, Make and Microsoft Power Automate product documentation on approval steps.
  • Ethan Mollick, Co-Intelligence: Living and Working with AI, Portfolio, 2024.

quiz.q: Dana, a bookkeeper at a Tulsa plumbing company, uploads a 2,000-row invoice export and the AI reports revenue of $386,200. What should she do before the figure goes into the owner's report?
opts: Round the figure to the nearest thousand so that any small errors disappear
Paste the number into the report and note that AI produced it
Ask the assistant to state the figure again with more confidence
Recalculate the total with a spreadsheet formula and compare row counts
quiz.x: An independent recalculation and row count catch skipped or misread rows. Labeling the number as AI-produced is honest but leaves a possible error in the report.

quiz.q: Luis, a paralegal in Toronto, uploads a scanned 60-page lease, and the AI summary skips renewal terms he knows are on page 41. What is the most likely cause and fix?
opts: The lease is too recent for the model; wait for the next version to be released
The assistant dislikes legal language; rephrase the request in a friendlier tone
The scan is an image without readable text; run OCR and ask for page-cited answers
The file name confused the tool; rename the lease and upload the very same scan again
quiz.x: Scanned PDFs are often pictures of text, so OCR plus page citations addresses the cause. Re-uploading the same scan under a new name changes nothing the tool can read.

quiz.q: Priya, an HR coordinator in Minneapolis, asks an AI to summarize a 90-page benefits guide and plans to email that summary to 300 employees. Which step best protects her?
opts: Request page references and verify each key claim against the guide
Ask for a shorter summary so there is less text that could be wrong
Send it with a disclaimer that the content came from an AI tool
Ask the AI whether it is sure that its summary is fully accurate
quiz.x: Page references let her confirm the claims that matter against the source. A disclaimer warns readers but does not stop a wrong deductible or deadline from reaching 300 people.

quiz.q: A Vancouver yoga studio owner wants an AI-made poster showing the class schedule, prices in CAD and the studio's logo. Which plan fits what image tools do well today?
opts: Generate the full poster and trust the prices as rendered in the image
Generate the background art, then add text and logo in a design tool
Ask the image tool to recreate the logo from a written description
Generate ten posters and pick whichever one has the fewest typos
quiz.x: Image tools are strong at artwork and weaker at exact text and logos, so adding those afterward is reliable. Picking the version with the fewest typos still publishes typos.

quiz.q: A volunteer at an Ohio nonprofit wants to generate a realistic picture of a named city council member shaking hands with the director for the spring newsletter. What is the best response?
opts: Use a real photo with permission; a fake one could mislead readers
Generate it and add a small caption saying the event was imagined
Generate it but blur the faces slightly so it looks less realistic
Generate it, since public officials have fewer privacy protections
quiz.x: A realistic image of a real person at an event that did not happen can deceive and harm, which breaks Do no harm. A small caption is easy to miss or crop out when the image is shared.

quiz.q: Marcus records a 45-minute client call at a Chicago marketing agency and wants an AI transcript with action items. Which step should come before anything is uploaded?
opts: Delete the audio after transcribing so no one can check the quotes
Confirm everyone on the call agreed to recording and AI processing
Ask the AI to guess speaker names from the sound of their voices
Upload the audio to whichever free transcription site loads fastest
quiz.x: Consent rules for recording vary by state and province, and client data deserves an approved tool. Picking the fastest free site skips both the consent and the privacy question.

quiz.q: After a board meeting at a Halifax credit union, the AI transcript shows a motion passing '15 to 2', but the secretary remembers a much closer vote. What is the sensible next step?
opts: Average the two numbers and record the result as an estimate
Ask the AI to regenerate the transcript until the vote looks right
Keep the transcript figure, since software hears better than people
Replay that part of the recording and correct the minutes by hand
quiz.x: Transcription often mishears numbers, and the recording is the source of truth. Regenerating until it looks right swaps one unverified guess for another.

quiz.q: Elena, a grant writer in Sacramento, retypes the same background about her nonprofit, its tone and its formatting rules at the start of each chat. Which feature addresses this?
opts: An image generator that turns the formatting rules into a visual guide
A longer first prompt typed from memory at the start of each new chat session
A saved setup such as custom instructions or a project with reference files
A voice mode conversation so she can speak the background more quickly
quiz.x: Custom instructions or a project store persona, tone, format and reference files once. Speaking the background by voice is quicker than typing but she still repeats it every time.

quiz.q: A school counselor in Texas wants to load student records into a shared custom assistant so teachers can ask questions about individual students. What should happen first?
opts: Share the assistant by link so no one needs a separate login to use it
Remove student last names and upload everything else as it stands
Check district policy and FERPA guidance, and keep identifiable data out
Upload the records, then remind teachers to use the assistant carefully
quiz.x: Student records may be protected, so policy and approved tools come before any upload. Removing last names alone usually leaves students identifiable through other details.

quiz.q: Jordan runs a five-person HVAC company in Phoenix and wants new web-form leads to receive an AI-drafted reply automatically. Which first design is the safest starting point?
opts: The AI sends replies overnight when fewer customers are watching
The AI replies and also quotes prices so customers can book faster
The AI sends replies instantly and he reviews a sample of them once a month
The draft lands in his inbox, and he approves each one before it sends
quiz.x: An approval step keeps a human in the loop while trust is built. Monthly sampling finds mistakes weeks after customers have already received them.

facts.t: Row count, one total, one sample before you trust an AI's numbers.
facts.more: Compare the rows the assistant says it read with your file, recalculate one headline figure with a formula, and trace one row by hand. It takes about five minutes.

facts.t: Optical character recognition turns a picture of text into readable text.
facts.more: If you cannot select the words in a PDF, it is probably a scan. Without OCR, an assistant may miss some or all of the content.

facts.t: VisiCalc, the first spreadsheet program for personal computers, was released.
facts.more: Spreadsheets have done reliable arithmetic for decades. Let the spreadsheet calculate and let AI help you find and explain the story.

facts.t: Trigger, AI draft, human approval, action.
facts.more: A safe first automation has the AI prepare a draft and a person approve it. Keep that approval step until the drafts have a long record of needing no changes.

labs.title: Audit this AI data summary

I asked it for the Excel formula so I could check the late-payment count myself.

plaibox.title: Simulation: your first automation
plaibox.intro: You manage the front office at a dental practice in Columbus, Ohio, and want to automate replies to new-patient inquiries. Scoring: 2 = best practice, 1 = partial, 0 = risky.
plaibox.win: Well designed. Your automation drafts quickly, a person approves, and patient information stays protected.
plaibox.lose: Revisit the design. Start small, keep an approval step, and check privacy rules before any patient data flows through a tool.

steps.s: Which task do you automate first?
o: Drafting replies to general new-patient inquiries
Frequent, low risk and easy to review. A good first automation.
Answering questions about a patient's treatment and insurance claim
That involves health information and clinical judgment. Keep it with staff.
Posting daily to the practice's social media accounts with no review
Low privacy risk, but unreviewed public posts can embarrass the practice.

steps.s: The inquiry form collects name, phone and a free-text box where people sometimes describe symptoms. What do you do?
o: Send the full form to any AI tool; it is just an inquiry
Symptoms tied to a name may be protected health information. Check first.
Ask the practice's privacy lead which tools are approved
Rules such as HIPAA may apply. Approved tools and agreements come first.
Send only the first name and the free-text box to the AI step
Less data is better, but the text box can still identify a person and a condition.

steps.s: The AI step has drafted a reply. Where does it go?
o: Straight to the patient so the response time looks impressive
No human in the loop. A wrong hour or price goes out under your name.
To a shared inbox as a draft for staff to approve
Staff edit and send. Speed from the AI, judgment from a person.
Straight to the patient, with a copy to you for later reading
You will see errors, but only after the patient has.

steps.s: After two weeks, 9 of 10 drafts needed no edits. One quoted a cleaning price that was out of date. Next move?
o: Remove the approval step, since 90% is a strong result
One wrong price in ten is too many to send unreviewed.
Tell the AI to stop mentioning prices and keep approvals
Fix the cause, keep the gate, and keep measuring.
Turn the automation off and go back to typing every reply
Safe, but you lose a real time saving over a fixable problem.

modules.t: Class 6 — Your AI playbook: a 30-day plan and where to go next
modules.d: Build a personal AI playbook with three recurring tasks, a prompt library, honest time-saved measurement and a responsible-use checklist, then present it and choose your next step.
modules.body:
This is the capstone class. You leave with a one-page AI playbook: three recurring tasks, a tested prompt for each, an honest measure of time saved, and your own rules for responsible use. A playbook beats a list of tools because it is built around your work, and it still makes sense when the tools change.

Class agenda (90 minutes)

  • 0:00-0:10 Quick review: the 3 Commandments of AI and the CLEAR prompt elements
  • 0:10-0:25 Pick your three recurring tasks
  • 0:25-0:45 Build your prompt library and workflow (Lab 1)
  • 0:45-0:55 Measuring time saved honestly, with a worked example
  • 0:55-1:05 Your responsible-use checklist (Lab 2)
  • 1:05-1:25 Playbook presentations in small groups, scored with the rubric
  • 1:25-1:30 Staying current and next steps

Step 1: Pick three recurring tasks

Look back over your last two weeks of work and list tasks you repeat. Choose three that pass these tests:

  • Recurring: you do it at least weekly, or monthly if it is long.
  • Language-heavy: writing, summarizing, sorting, planning or explaining.
  • Reviewable: you can tell in a few minutes whether the output is good.
  • Low risk: a mistake caught in review costs little, and no restricted data is needed.

Good candidates include a weekly status email, meeting notes turned into action items, a first draft of a parent newsletter, or replies to common customer questions. Leave out hiring decisions, performance reviews, medical or legal judgments, and anything your employer has told you to keep out of AI tools.

Step 2: Build a prompt library and a workflow

A prompt library is a document where you keep prompts that worked. A notes app or a single shared doc is enough. For each task, save an entry with:

  1. A job-based name, such as "Weekly schedule email".
  2. The prompt, written with the CLEAR elements: Persona, Tone, Format, Details and Target audience.
  3. [Bracketed variables] for what changes each time, such as [dates] or [client name].
  4. The Context or Reference material to attach, such as last week's version.
  5. Your review step: what you check before using the output.

The workflow is the order you follow: gather inputs, run the saved prompt, Iterate once or twice, Evaluate against your review step, then send or file. Write it as four or five short lines beside the prompt so you can follow it on a busy day.

🧪 Interactive Lab — try it now

Help me turn a recurring task into a reusable prompt library entry. My task is: [describe the task, how often you do it, and who receives the result]. Ask me up to four questions about the persona you should adopt, the tone, the format, the details to include, and the target audience. Then write (1) a reusable prompt with [bracketed variables] for anything that changes each time, (2) a list of what I should attach as context or reference, and (3) a three-item review checklist I should complete before I use the output.

Step 3: Measure time saved honestly (worked example)

Maria manages the office at a dental practice in Calgary. Each week she writes the staff schedule email.

  • Baseline: she times three normal weeks and averages 40 minutes.
  • With AI: 5 minutes to gather inputs and run her saved prompt, plus 10 minutes to review and fix, for 15 minutes.
  • Net saving: 40 minus 15 is 25 minutes a week.
  • Setup: she spent 60 minutes building and testing the prompt.

Over her first four weeks Maria saves 100 minutes and spent 60 on setup, so her net gain is 40 minutes. From then on she gains about 25 minutes a week. If you count drafting time alone, the saving looks like 35 minutes a week. That overstates it by 40 percent, because review is part of the job.

Record quality as well. Did the output need heavy edits? Did anyone notice a difference? If a task saves no time after three honest tries, drop it from your playbook and pick another. A dropped task is a useful finding.

Key takeaway: Honest time saved = baseline minus (prompting time + review and fix time), with setup time subtracted once. Measure before you start, or you will be guessing.

Step 4: Your responsible-use checklist

Write your checklist in your own words and keep it on the same page as your prompts. A starting version built on the 3 Commandments:

  • Investigate, understand, apply: I know which tools my employer approves, and I have read how my tool handles the data I give it.
  • Review for hallucinations: I verify names, numbers, dates, quotes and citations against a source before anything leaves my desk.
  • Do no harm: I keep personal, client, patient and student information out unless policy and the tool allow it. Laws such as HIPAA, FERPA or PIPEDA may apply to my role; when unsure, I ask.
  • I am open about AI help where my audience or employer expects it.
  • Decisions about people stay with a person.
🧪 Interactive Lab — try it now

Act as a practical workplace AI coach. I work as a [job title] at a [type of organization] in [state or province]. Draft a personal responsible-use checklist of seven items or fewer, organized under three headings: Investigate, understand, apply; Review for hallucinations and keep a human in the loop; Do no harm. Make each item a specific action I can tick off. Flag any item where I should confirm my employer's policy or a privacy rule, and state plainly that this is general guidance, not legal advice.

Your 30-day plan

  • Week 1: time your three tasks the usual way to set baselines. Draft a prompt for each.
  • Week 2: use the prompts on real work. Log minutes and edits each time.
  • Week 3: improve the weakest prompt, add reference material, and save a reusable setup if your tool offers one.
  • Week 4: total your results, drop or replace anything that is not paying off, and share your playbook with one colleague.

Staying current without chasing every tool

New AI products appear every week, and most will not change your work. Choose one main assistant and learn it well. Follow one or two reliable sources, such as your tool's release notes and a trusted newsletter. Once a month, spend 30 minutes retesting your saved prompts and trying one new feature. Before switching tools, ask one question: would this beat my current setup on one of my three tasks?

Presenting your playbook: capstone rubric

You have five minutes. Show one task before and after, share your numbers, and name one thing that did not work.

  • Task selection and baselines (15%): three recurring, reviewable, low-risk tasks, each timed.
  • Prompt library (25%): three saved prompts using CLEAR elements and variables.
  • Workflow with human review (20%): clear steps and a named review check.
  • Honest measurement (20%): review and setup time counted; quality noted.
  • Responsible-use checklist (10%): specific, personal, tied to the 3 Commandments.
  • Presentation (10%): clear, on time, candid about limits.

Where to go next

  • AI Unlocked Professional: Team21's next level, moving from single prompts to repeatable systems, deeper techniques and working with your own knowledge sources.
  • Role specializations: applied tracks for particular kinds of work, such as education, business and nonprofit roles.
  • Builder tracks: for learners who want to create automations, custom assistants and simple tools.

Ask your instructor for the current catalog and schedule, since offerings are updated over time.

📚 Glossary

  • Playbook: a one-page record of your tasks, prompts, workflow, measurements and rules.
  • Prompt library: a saved, named collection of prompts that have worked for you.
  • Variable: a [bracketed] placeholder in a prompt that you replace each time.
  • Baseline: how long a task takes before you change how you do it.
  • Net time saved: baseline minus all time spent with AI, including review, fixes and setup.
  • Rubric: a scoring guide that lists criteria and how much each one counts.
  • Capstone: a final project that brings a course's skills together.

📖 References

  • National Institute of Standards and Technology, AI Risk Management Framework (AI RMF 1.0), 2023.
  • Ethan Mollick, Co-Intelligence: Living and Working with AI, Portfolio, 2024.
  • Stanford Institute for Human-Centered AI, AI Index Report (annual).
  • Official documentation and release notes for your assistant (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Microsoft); features and plans change often.
  • U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HIPAA), U.S. Department of Education (FERPA), and Office of the Privacy Commissioner of Canada (PIPEDA) guidance pages.

quiz.q: Renee, an office manager at a Portland architecture firm, must pick three tasks for her 30-day AI plan. Which of these sets is the strongest choice for a first playbook?
opts: Weekly status email, meeting notes cleanup, and vendor follow-up messages
Whatever tasks come up during the month, chosen as each one appears
Final hiring decisions, salary reviews, and employee discipline letters too
Annual holiday party plan, a one-time office move, and a logo redesign
quiz.x: Recurring, reviewable, low-risk tasks give enough repetitions to measure. One-time projects may feel bigger, but they offer nothing to compare week over week.

quiz.q: Tom, a real estate agent in Ottawa, wrote a prompt that produced an excellent listing description last week but cannot find it now. Which habit would have prevented this?
opts: Writing a fresh prompt each time so the wording stays more creative
Saving it right away under a job-based name with [bracketed] variables
Asking the AI to remember the prompt for him across all future sessions
Relying on the chat history sidebar to surface it when it is needed
quiz.x: A named library entry with variables is easy to find and reuse on any tool. Chat history is hard to search and memory features vary by product and plan.

quiz.q: Aisha, a billing specialist at a Detroit clinic, says AI cut her monthly report from 3 hours to 20 minutes, but she spends 50 minutes fixing errors afterward. What is her honest time saved?
opts: About 160 minutes, since fixing errors is a separate job from drafting
About 180 minutes, since the AI now does the whole report for her
About 110 minutes, since review and fixes count as part of the task
It cannot be estimated until she has a full year of timing records
quiz.x: 180 minus (20 + 50) is 110 minutes. The 160-minute figure counts drafting alone and leaves out the review work that makes the report usable.

quiz.q: Before starting his 30-day plan, Carlos, a logistics coordinator in Winnipeg, wants to prove whether AI helps with shipment update emails. What should he record first?
opts: How long the job takes now, timed across three or four normal runs
How long he expects the task to take once the AI is doing most of it
How confident he feels about prompting after finishing the course
How many AI tools his coworkers have tried during the past quarter
quiz.x: A measured baseline is the comparison point for any saving. An expected time is a hope, and without the before number it cannot be tested.

quiz.q: A nurse educator at a Seattle hospital wants to paste a patient case with name and birth date into a consumer chatbot to draft teaching notes. Which checklist item applies first?
opts: Use the case as written, because teaching is an allowed purpose
Strip identifiers or use an approved tool, per hospital privacy policy
Add a line asking the chatbot to keep the patient details confidential
Paste the case late at night when fewer people are using the service
quiz.x: Identifiable patient data may be protected under rules such as HIPAA, so it stays out of unapproved tools. Asking a chatbot to keep it confidential does not change where the data goes.

quiz.q: Greg, a sales manager in Atlanta, plans to send an AI-written proposal quoting a market-size statistic he has not seen anywhere else. Which of the 3 Commandments is most directly at stake?
opts: Investigate, understand, apply, since he should learn more AI tools
Do no harm, since proposals can sometimes disappoint a customer
None of them, since statistics fall outside what the rules cover
Review for hallucinations and keep a human in the loop before sending
quiz.x: An unverified statistic is a classic hallucination risk, so checking the source comes first. Do no harm is related, but the harm here is prevented by the review step.

quiz.q: Nadia, a small-business owner in Edmonton, feels behind because a new AI app trends on social media nearly every week. Which routine fits this course's advice on staying current?
opts: A pause on AI use until the market settles on a single clear winner
A short monthly review that retests her saved prompts on her main tool
A daily hour of testing each new app before her competitors find it
A switch to whichever assistant ranks highest on this week's leaderboard
quiz.x: A monthly check keeps her skills and prompts current at low cost. Switching with each leaderboard change resets her setup and saved work again and again.

quiz.q: In her five-minute capstone presentation, Olivia, a program officer at a Boston foundation, has time to show one thing in depth. Which choice best demonstrates her playbook?
opts: A slide listing the many features of her favorite AI assistant
A tour of the AI tools she signed up for during the six classes
One task shown before and after, with timings and her review step
A reading of her longest prompt from the first word to the very last
quiz.x: A before-and-after with numbers and a review step shows the full workflow and its result. Reading a prompt aloud shows the input without evidence that it works.

quiz.q: A capstone rubric gives 25% to the prompt library and 10% to presentation polish. Ben, a teacher in Buffalo, has two hours left to prepare. Where should most of that time go?
opts: Testing and tightening his three prompts so each has clear variables
Adding animations and a custom color theme to his presentation slides
Collecting screenshots of AI tools that he did not end up using
Rehearsing his opening joke until the timing feels natural to him
quiz.x: Weights show where effort pays off, and the library carries more than twice the weight of polish. Slide design helps a little but sits in the smallest category.

quiz.q: After the course, Hannah, an operations lead at a Raleigh insurance agency, uses AI daily for emails and now hopes to build a small tool that routes customer requests. Which next step fits her goal?
opts: A general news subscription, since tools change quickly these days
Repeating the foundations class, since repetition builds confidence
Waiting a year, since building is best left to trained engineers
A builder track, since she wants to create workflows and simple tools
quiz.x: Her goal is to build, which matches a builder track. Repeating foundations would strengthen skills she already uses daily without moving her toward routing requests.

facts.t: A first playbook covers three recurring, reviewable, low-risk tasks.
facts.more: Three is enough to see a pattern and few enough to measure properly. Add a fourth only after these are working.

facts.t: Saving 10 minutes each workday adds up over a year.
facts.more: 10 minutes x 5 days x 52 weeks = 2,600 minutes, or about 43 hours. Small, honest savings on frequent tasks beat a big saving on a rare one.

facts.t: The capstone rubric weights: 15, 25, 20, 20, 10 and 10.
facts.more: Prompt library 25%, workflow 20% and honest measurement 20% carry most of the score. Presentation polish is 10%.

facts.t: The NIST AI Risk Management Framework: Govern, Map, Measure, Manage.
facts.more: NIST released AI RMF 1.0 in January 2023 as voluntary guidance. Your personal checklist is a one-person version of the same idea.
